title: Broadband Quantum Optical Storage with Chemically Engineered Molecular Eu$^\text{3+}$ Complex
authors: Yisheng Lei, Senthil Kumar Kuppusamy, Idris Tlemsani, Suma Al-Hunaishi, Pengrui Jiao, Olaf Fuhr, Mario Ruben, Philippe Goldner, Diana Serrano
abstract: Broadband quantum memory devices are essential elements for future quantum networks. Here we propose a broadband quantum memory scheme called Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) for rare-earth ions in solids. We provide a Eu$^\text{3+}$ molecular complex with special hyperfine level structures of which the hyperfine level separations are in a specific mathematical correlation that can be obtained by harnessing chemical engineering. Using the memory protocol and material, we experimentally demonstrate a quantum optical storage efficiency of 14.9% and a memory bandwidth of 200MHz, which can easily be extended to a few GHz. With this demonstration, we show the first quantum application enabled by molecular engineering which cannot be achieved by any other existing Eu$^\text{3+}$ solid-state materials. In addition, we provide a framework for the chemical engineering of solid-state materials with rare-earth ions for quantum applications consisting of material design, synthesis & characterization techniques, and analytical methods for the quantum properties of rare-earth (RE) ions in solids. This work establishes a new direction in which molecular rare-earth ions can be used for a wide range of quantum applications, which cannot be realized by existing solid-state materials. This will greatly facilitate the development of molecular quantum emitter systems for real world applications.
summary: This paper proposes and experimentally demonstrates a novel quantum memory scheme, HAGEM, using $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ ions engineered within molecular complexes. By chemically tailoring the hyperfine structure, the authors achieved high quantum optical storage efficiency and bandwidth. This establishes a new paradigm where molecular engineering enables quantum applications unattainable with conventional solid-state rare-earth materials.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a broadband quantum memory device essential for future quantum networks.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a quantum optical storage efficiency of 14.9% and a memory bandwidth of 200 MHz using a novel molecularly engineered $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ complex.
method: The work combines theoretical modeling of hyperfine structures with experimental demonstrations using spectral hole burning and quantum optical storage protocols.
model_or_system: The system utilizes $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ ions embedded in molecular complexes, employing the Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) protocol, which relies on specific correlations in hyperfine level separations.
key_observables: Quantum optical storage efficiency (14.9%), memory bandwidth (200 MHz), hyperfine level separations ($\delta$), and spectral grating structure.
important_parameters: Memory bandwidth (extendable to GHz), hyperfine level structure correlations, and the coupling between molecular engineering and quantum memory function.
main_assumptions: The protocol requires specific hyperfine level structures that are engineered into the molecular complex, overcoming limitations of naturally occurring solid-state materials.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the HAGEM memory protocol, showing spectral hole burning simulations and the resulting broadband spectrum achievable with the designed $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ complex.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for broadband quantum memory, proposing the HAGEM scheme, detailing the molecular engineering approach using $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ complexes, and finally presenting experimental demonstrations of storage efficiency and bandwidth.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum networking by providing a solid-state platform for quantum memory, bridging the gap between molecular chemistry and quantum information science.
